title: Survival and swim speed performance of Alewife, a small, laterally compressed prey fish, following acoustic transmitter implantation
content:
Abstract

Alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus) is a small, pelagic fish that is an important prey source for piscivores in the Laurentian Great Lakes, yet its spatial ecology is poorly known, which limits the ability to monitor populations. Acoustic telemetry is a tool to understand spatial ecology; however, there may be tagging effects on a smaller body-sized population of Alewife where tag burden is higher than in larger-bodied marine populations. We assessed survival, swimming abilities and healing of Alewife from Lake Ontario after acoustic transmitter implantation. In a laboratory setting, tagged Alewife were compared across tag sizes (Innovasea models V6 and V7-4x), controls and shams (surgery conducted with no tag implantation) in fall 2024 (n = 76). Tagging survival was also assessed in spring 2025 (variety of V7 tags) when Alewife had developed gonads and across sex (n = 126). Capture, transport and laboratory introduction resulted in moderate mortality in fall 2024 (40%), which was reduced in spring 2025 (4%), an improvement we attribute to the refined protocols reported here. Post-treatment (transmitter, sham, control) survival was high (100% in fall; 91% in spring) with tag burdens from 2 to 8%. We attribute lower spring survival to gonad development, but it was also influenced significantly by a holding tank effect. Two weeks post-tagging, Alewife achieved critical swimming speeds of 37.9 ± 7.6 cm s−1, with no significant differences among treatments. Incisions were all scored as moderately to highly healed 2 weeks post-surgery. Our findings establish the feasibility of tagging smaller, freshwater Alewife with acoustic tags, following best practices reported here, for telemetry applications in the Great Lakes to better understand the spatial ecology of this lower trophic species of major management and ecosystem importance.
